subject: mathematics_2a
question_text: Solve x⁴ + x³ − 16x² − 4x + 48 = 0, given that the product of two of the roots is 6.

mark_split.label: Name the roots; αβ = 6 gives γδ = 8
Write the quartic as two quadratic factors with sums p, q
Expand, compare coefficients, find p and q
Solve both quadratics and list the roots

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Senior Inter Maths-2A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.92 — Star Questions Plus, Theory of Equations banner, answer 195. Printed appearances: TS 19. Paper position: Maths-2A Section C runs Q18–Q24 at 7 marks each, answer any 5 of 7; Q19 is the Theory of Equations slot (blueprint, book p.3; all five model papers pp.111–120 agree). This question appears in none of the five model papers. Truth check: (x² − 5x + 6)(x² + 6x + 8) expands to x⁴ + x³ − 16x² − 4x + 48; the roots 2, 3, −2, −4 add to −1 = −a₁/a₀ and multiply to 48 = a₄/a₀, and 2 · 3 = 6 as given. recall_prompt: Say how you would solve this — what the product 6 tells you about the other pair, how the two pairs become two quadratic factors, and how you find the pair-sums.
insider_note: Only the x³ and x coefficients are needed to find p and q; the x² coefficient is a free check that most students never write.

steps.label: Name the roots
steps.margin_note: First mark. Call the roots α, β, γ, δ with αβ = 6. The product of all four is the constant term 48 (a₀ = 1, even degree so the sign is +), which forces γδ = 8.
lines: Let the roots be α, β, γ, δ with αβ = 6.
Product of all four: αβγδ = a₄/a₀ = 48,

recall.must_convey: That the roots are named with αβ = 6, and that since αβγδ = 48 the other pair has product γδ = 8.

the two given roots multiply to six and all four multiply to forty eight so the other two multiply to eight
split the product forty eight as six times eight

steps.why: The product of all the roots of a monic quartic is its constant term (with a + sign, because the degree is even). Knowing one pair's product therefore fixes the other pair's product at once — that is the whole reason the question gives you 6.
common_mistakes: Writing αβγδ = −48 (the sign is + for even degree: (−1)⁴ a₄/a₀).
Not naming which two roots have product 6, so nothing can be paired later.

steps.label: Two quadratic factors
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Let the two pair-sums be p and q. Each pair is the root set of a quadratic x² − (sum)x + product, so the quartic is the product of x² − px + 6 and x² − qx + 8.
lines: Let α + β = p and γ + δ = q.
The quadratic with roots α, β: x² − px + 6
The quadratic with roots γ, δ: x² − qx + 8

recall.must_convey: That with α + β = p and γ + δ = q, the quartic factorises as (x² − px + 6)(x² − qx + 8).
accept: let alpha plus beta be p and gamma plus delta be q, then the quartic is x squared minus p x plus six times x squared minus q x plus eight
each pair gives a quadratic with its sum and product, and the quartic is the product of the two
write the quartic as two quadratic factors with unknown sums p and q
pair sums p, q ga pettali, quartic ante x square minus p x plus six into x square minus q x plus eight
the two quadratics have products six and eight and sums p and q
heard_as: x squared minus p x plus six
x squared minus q x plus eight

steps.why: A root pair with known product needs only its sum to become a quadratic factor. Naming those two sums p and q turns a four-unknown problem into a two-unknown one, and the quartic must equal the product of the two factors.
common_mistakes: Putting the products in the wrong factors (6 goes with p, 8 with q).
Writing x² + px + 6 (the middle sign is minus the sum).

steps.label: Compare coefficients
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Expand, then match x³ (p + q = −1) and x (8p + 6q = 4). Solve the pair: p = 5, q = −6. Check on the x² coefficient: pq + 14 = −16.

recall.must_convey: That expanding and comparing the x³ and x coefficients gives p + q = −1 and 8p + 6q = 4, solved to p = 5 and q = −6, with the x² coefficient as a check.
accept: expand and compare, p plus q is minus one and eight p plus six q is four, so p is five and q is minus six
match the x cubed and x coefficients to get two equations in p and q and solve them
comparing coefficients gives p equals five and q equals minus six, and the x squared term checks
coefficients compare chesthe p plus q minus one, eight p plus six q four, p five q minus six
two linear equations in p and q from the expansion

steps.why: Two unknowns need two equations; the x³ and x coefficients give the two simplest ones. The x² coefficient is a third equation that costs nothing to check and catches any slip in p and q.
common_mistakes: A sign slip: the x³ coefficient of the product is −(p + q), so p + q = −1, not +1.
The x coefficient is −(8p + 6q) (each sum times the OTHER pair's product).
Solving for p and never checking with the x² coefficient.

steps.label: Solve both quadratics
steps.margin_note: Last two marks. x² − 5x + 6 factorises as (x − 2)(x − 3) and x² + 6x + 8 as (x + 2)(x + 4). The pair 2, 3 has product 6 as required; all four add to −1.

recall.must_convey: That the two quadratics x² − 5x + 6 and x² + 6x + 8 are solved to give the four roots 2, 3, −2, −4.
accept: solve x squared minus five x plus six and x squared plus six x plus eight, the roots are two three minus two minus four
the two quadratics factorise to give two and three, and minus two and minus four
the four roots are two, three, minus two and minus four

steps.why: Once p and q are known both factors are ordinary quadratics. The root pair 2, 3 has product 6, which is the condition the question gave — writing that check is what shows the pairing was right.
common_mistakes: Solving only one of the two quadratics.
Not checking that one pair really multiplies to 6.
